sections.b: Luke tells Jesus' birth from Mary's side. Gabriel greets her as one God has favored (Luke 1:28–30), promises a son who will reign on David's throne, and answers her question "since I do not know a man?" with the Holy Spirit's overshadowing (Luke 1:34–35). Her reply, "Here is the Lord's slave" (Luke 1:38), makes her the first to believe the good news. Elizabeth calls her "my Lord's mother" and blessed for her faith (Luke 1:43–45), and Mary sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55). She treasures and ponders what happens (Luke 2:19, 51), hears Simeon's warning of a sword (Luke 2:35), and does not understand her twelve-year-old son's answer (Luke 2:48–50). Luke's Mary is both chosen mother and model disciple (Luke 8:21; 11:27–28; Acts 1:14).

common: The words of the Hail Mary's first half come from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.
uncommon: A few Latin manuscripts give the Magnificat to Elizabeth, and some scholars have argued she was its original singer.

sections.b: Luke tells the virginal conception through a dialogue: Mary, promised in marriage but not yet living with Joseph, asks how she can conceive "since I do not know a man" (Luke 1:34), and the angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come on her and the Most High's power will overshadow her, so the child will be called God's Son (Luke 1:35). Luke's wording echoes the Greek of Isaiah 7:13–14 (virgin, house of David, conceive, son) without quoting it, unlike Matthew 1:23. On the majority view that Luke did not know Matthew, the two tell independent stories and agree on this point, which most scholars take as evidence that the belief is older than both Gospels. Luke still calls Joseph Jesus' father and the two "his parents" (Luke 2:27, 33, 41, 48), since Joseph is his legal father; later scribes sometimes changed these words.
sections.refs: Luke 1:26–38; Luke 2:5; Luke 2:33; Luke 2:43; Luke 3:23; Isaiah 7:13–14; Matthew 1:18–25

uncommon: Mary's question in Luke 1:34 shows that she had vowed lifelong virginity (Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine).

sections.b: Only Luke tells of John's birth. He is a priest's son on both sides (Luke 1:5), announced by Gabriel in the sanctuary as one who will go ahead of the Lord "with Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17), filled with the Spirit before birth, who leaps in the womb at Mary's greeting (Luke 1:15, 41, 44). His name, "the LORD has been gracious," breaks family custom (Luke 1:59–63), and his father's song names him "a prophet of the Most High" who will prepare the Lord's roads (Luke 1:76). He grows up in the wilderness until his public appearance (Luke 1:80), where some scholars place him near the Qumran community. Luke pairs him with Jesus throughout, always as the lesser.

Luke dates Jesus' birth by a registration ordered by Augustus "while Quirinius governed Syria" (Luke 2:1–2), which brought Joseph from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Josephus dates Quirinius' census of Judea to AD 6, after Herod's son Archelaus was deposed, and it sparked the revolt of Judas the Galilean, which Luke also knows (Acts 5:37). Since Luke and Matthew both place the birth under Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC, the date is a famous difficulty. Most critical scholars think Luke conflated the two; others propose an earlier registration, an earlier post for Quirinius, or the translation "before Quirinius governed."

Luke calls Bethlehem "David's town" (Luke 2:4, 11), a title the Old Testament gives to Jerusalem's fortress (2 Samuel 5:7). Joseph goes there because he is of David's house. Mary lays the newborn in a manger "since there was no space for them in the guest room" (Luke 2:7): the word is kataluma, a guest room or lodging, as in Luke 22:11, not a commercial inn, and there is no innkeeper in the text. Kenneth Bailey argued that the family stayed in a crowded village house where animals were kept at one end. From the second century a cave near Bethlehem was shown as the birthplace (Justin Martyr), where the Church of the Nativity now stands.

sections.h: Zechariah and the division of Abijah
sections.b: Luke's story opens with a priest of the eighth division, Abijah (1 Chronicles 24:10), serving his week in the temple. The lot fell to him to burn the incense in the sanctuary (Luke 1:8–9), an honor the Mishnah says a priest could receive only once in a lifetime (Mishnah Tamid 5:2). While the people prayed outside at the hour of incense, Gabriel appeared to him beside the altar (Luke 1:10–11). After his days of service he went home to the hill country (Luke 1:23, 39).

Angels are more active in Luke 1–2 than anywhere else in the Gospels. Gabriel, named elsewhere in the Bible only in Daniel 8–9, "stands before God" and brings the two birth announcements (Luke 1:19, 26). An angel of the Lord announces Jesus' birth to shepherds, and "a crowd of heaven's army" praises God (Luke 2:9–14). After the birth stories angels nearly vanish from Luke until the empty tomb (Luke 24:4, 23), framing Jesus' life.

Elizabeth is the last of the Bible's barren mothers. Righteous but childless, she and Zechariah are "well along in their days" (Luke 1:7), echoing Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18:11). When she conceives she hides herself for five months and thanks God for taking away her "disgrace among people" (Luke 1:25), Rachel's words (Genesis 30:23). The angel offers her pregnancy as a sign to Mary: "People called her barren, yet this is her sixth month" (Luke 1:36). Luke pairs a woman too old to conceive with a virgin who has not yet known a man, so that the second miracle surpasses the first.

Luke's birth stories echo the story of Samuel throughout. Mary's song follows Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1–10): God lifts the lowly and humbles the mighty, fills the hungry and empties the full. Mary's "he has looked ... on the lowliness of his slave" (Luke 1:48) repeats almost word for word the Greek of Hannah's vow (1 Samuel 1:11). Jesus is presented in the temple as Samuel was given to the LORD at Shiloh (Luke 2:22; 1 Samuel 1:24–28), an old man blesses the parents in both stories (Eli; Simeon, who expects to die soon, Luke 2:29), the prophetess is named Anna (Hannah), and Jesus grows "in favor with God and with people" as the boy Samuel did (Luke 2:52; 1 Samuel 2:26).
sections.refs: Luke 1:46–55; Luke 2:22–38; Luke 2:52; 1 Samuel 1:11; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; 1 Samuel 2:26

sections.h: The promise to David in Luke 1–2
sections.b: Gabriel's message to Mary restates God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16): "The Lord God will hand him the throne of David his father, and he will be king over Jacob's house for all the ages. His kingdom will have no end" (Luke 1:32–33). Zechariah praises God for raising "a horn of salvation" in David's house (Luke 1:69; Psalm 132:17). Joseph is of David's house (Luke 1:27; 2:4), the birth is in David's town (Luke 2:11), and the child is "the Lord's Messiah" (Luke 2:26). Acts later presents the resurrection as the fulfillment of this promise (Acts 2:30–36).
sections.refs: Luke 1:27; Luke 1:32–33; Luke 1:69; Luke 2:4; Luke 2:11; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Acts 2:30–36

sections.h: "Son of the Most High" and "God's Son" in Luke 1
sections.b: Luke introduces Jesus' sonship in two steps. First he will be called "Son of the Most High" and receive David's throne (Luke 1:32), language for Israel's king, God's son by adoption (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), and strikingly close to the Aramaic Apocalypse (4Q246) from Qumran. Then, because the Holy Spirit and the Most High's power will bring about his conception, he will be called "God's Son" (Luke 1:35). At twelve Jesus himself speaks of God as "my Father" (Luke 2:49), and Luke's genealogy will end by tracing him back through Adam to God (Luke 3:38).
sections.refs: Luke 1:32–35; Luke 2:49; Luke 3:22; Luke 3:38; 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7

sections.b: The first use of christos in Luke is the angel's announcement to the shepherds: "a Savior was born for you in David's town. He is Messiah and Lord" (Luke 2:11), an unusual pair of titles that may echo "the Lord's anointed" (as in Luke 2:26). Luke 1–2 gathers Israel's messianic images: David's throne (Luke 1:32), a "horn of salvation" (Luke 1:69), the "Dawn from on high," which may also mean the messianic Branch (Luke 1:78), and the comfort of Israel and redemption of Jerusalem that Simeon and Anna await (Luke 2:25, 38).
sections.refs: Luke 1:32–33; Luke 1:69; Luke 1:78; Luke 2:11; Luke 2:25–26; Luke 2:38

sections.h: A Savior in the age of Augustus
sections.b: Luke sets Jesus' birth under Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:1), whom Greek cities honored as god and savior and whose birthday the Priene inscription (9 BC) called the beginning of "good news" for the world. Luke's angel uses the same vocabulary for a newborn in a manger: "good news," "a Savior," and the angels' "peace on earth" (Luke 2:10–14). Without calling for revolt, the story quietly gives the titles of the emperor to Jesus.

sections.h: Luke begins and ends in the temple
sections.b: Luke's Gospel opens in the sanctuary, where Zechariah burns incense (Luke 1:8–22), and closes with the disciples "continually in the temple" praising God (Luke 24:53). In between, the infant Jesus is presented in the temple and welcomed by Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38), and at twelve he stays among the teachers, calling it his Father's house (Luke 2:46–49). Luke distinguishes naos, the sanctuary building (Luke 1:9, 21), from hieron, the whole temple with its courts (Luke 2:27, 46).

Luke calls Jesus Mary's "firstborn" (Luke 2:7) and explains the presentation in the temple by the law that "every male that opens a womb will be called holy, belonging to the Lord" (Luke 2:23; Exodus 13:2, 12). Luke does not mention the five-shekel redemption price (Numbers 18:15–16); instead the scene recalls Hannah giving Samuel to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:24–28). The word "firstborn" itself does not settle whether Mary had later children.

Luke records that both John and Jesus were circumcised on the eighth day as the law commands (Luke 1:59; 2:21; Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), and both were named then, the earliest evidence for naming at circumcision, as Jews do today at the brit milah. Luke presents both families as faithful to the covenant of Abraham.

The first to hear of the Messiah's birth are shepherds keeping the night watch near Bethlehem, David's town, where David himself had kept sheep (Luke 2:8–20; 1 Samuel 16:11). They hurry to find the child, tell what they were told, and return praising God. Preachers often call them despised outcasts, citing later rabbinic texts; many scholars think Luke simply means humble working people, the lowly whom God lifts up (Luke 1:52).

Gabriel says John will go ahead of the Lord "with Elijah's spirit and power," to turn fathers' hearts back to their children (Luke 1:17), the promise of Malachi 4:5–6. Luke stops short of saying John is Elijah, as Matthew 11:14 and Mark 9:13 do, and elsewhere he links Jesus to Elijah as well (Luke 4:25–26; 7:11–17).

sections.h: The Spirit in Luke's birth stories
sections.b: Before the Spirit falls on the church in Acts 2, Luke shows the Spirit at work in faithful Israel. John will be filled with the Spirit before his birth (Luke 1:15), the Spirit will come on Mary and the Most High's power overshadow her (Luke 1:35), Elizabeth and Zechariah are filled with the Spirit and prophesy (Luke 1:41, 67), and the Spirit rests on Simeon, reveals to him that he will see the Messiah and leads him into the temple (Luke 2:25–27).
sections.refs: Luke 1:15; Luke 1:35; Luke 1:41; Luke 1:67; Luke 2:25–27; Acts 2:4

sections.b: Anna, married seven years and then a widow until eighty-four (or, on another reading, for eighty-four years), never left the temple, serving God with fasting and prayer night and day (Luke 2:36–37). If she was a widow for eighty-four years she would be about 105, the age of the widow Judith at her death (Judith 16:23). She is the first of several widows Luke presents with honor (Luke 4:25–26; 7:11–17; 18:1–8; 21:1–4).

sections.h: Anna of the tribe of Asher
sections.b: Luke says the prophetess Anna was "from Asher's tribe" (Luke 2:36), one of the northern tribes deported by Assyria. Her family had kept its tribal identity, as Tobit's family of Naphtali does in the book of Tobit, which shows that members of the northern tribes were still known in Jesus' time. Richard Bauckham suggests her family may have returned from the Asher community in Media.

Many Jews held that prophecy had ceased (1 Maccabees 9:27). Luke 1–2 is full of it: Elizabeth speaks by the Spirit (Luke 1:41–45), Zechariah "spoke as a prophet" (Luke 1:67), John will be "a prophet of the Most High" (Luke 1:76), Simeon prophesies (Luke 2:34–35) and Anna is a prophetess (Luke 2:36). Men and women prophesy alike, as Acts 2:17–18 promises.

sections.h: The poor in Luke's birth stories
sections.b: Luke's Gospel of the poor begins in its first chapters. Mary sings that God has raised the lowly and filled the hungry while sending the rich away empty (Luke 1:51–53). Jesus is laid in a manger (Luke 2:7), announced first to shepherds (Luke 2:8–20), and presented with the offering the law allowed for a mother who could not afford a lamb (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8).

Every year Jesus' parents went to Jerusalem for the Passover (Luke 2:41), as the law asked of Israelite men (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16), and families often went together. At twelve Jesus stayed behind in the temple; his parents found him "three days later" (Luke 2:46). Many readers see a foreshadowing of his last Passover journey to Jerusalem, his death and his rising on the third day (Luke 9:51; 22:1; 24:7).

Luke opens "back when Herod was king of Judea" (Luke 1:5), Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC; Matthew too places the birth in his reign (Matthew 2:1). Luke tells no story of Herod's hostility to the child. Herod's sons appear later in Luke: Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip (Luke 3:1; 23:7–12).

Luke makes Nazareth Mary's and Joseph's home before the birth: Gabriel is sent to "a Galilean town by the name of Nazareth" (Luke 1:26), the family returns there after the presentation (Luke 2:39), and Jesus grows up there under his parents' authority (Luke 2:51). In Matthew the family settles in Nazareth only after returning from Egypt (Matthew 2:22–23).

The Lord's glory, which once filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:11), shines around shepherds in the fields when Jesus' birth is announced (Luke 2:9), and the angels sing "Glory to God in the heights above" (Luke 2:14). Simeon calls the child "glory to Israel your people" (Luke 2:32; Isaiah 46:13).

sections.h: Jesus' birth and childhood in Luke
sections.b: Luke is the only Gospel that tells of Jesus' circumcision and naming (Luke 2:21), his presentation in the temple (Luke 2:22–38) and any event of his boyhood: at twelve he stays behind in the temple, listening to the teachers and asking them questions, and tells his parents he must be at his Father's (Luke 2:41–51). Luke frames the childhood with notes that he "kept growing and getting stronger" and "kept moving forward in wisdom and in maturity, and in favor with God and with people" (Luke 2:40, 52), affirming a real human growth that later theology had to account for.

sections.h: "Light to the nations, glory to Israel"
sections.b: Simeon sings that God's salvation is "a light to bring revelation to the nations, and glory to Israel your people" (Luke 2:32), joining Isaiah's promise to the nations (Isaiah 49:6) with Israel's own glory. He then warns that the child will cause "many in Israel to fall and to rise" (Luke 2:34). Interpreters of Luke-Acts disagree whether the two-volume work keeps this balance to the end (Jacob Jervell) or ends with Israel turned away and the nations turned to (Jack Sanders; Acts 28:28).

uncommon: Luke-Acts presents Jesus as Israel's restoration, with believing Gentiles added to a restored Israel, not replacing it (Jacob Jervell).

sections.b: The date of Jesus' birth is not given in the Bible. December 25 is first certainly attested in a Roman calendar of AD 354 (a passage of Hippolytus, about 204, giving December 25 may be earlier, if it is original), while many Eastern churches long kept January 6. Scholars debate whether the date was chosen to replace the Roman feast of the Unconquered Sun or calculated nine months after March 25, the traditional date of the Annunciation and of the crucifixion. Whether Christians should keep Christmas as a holy day at all was disputed at the Reformation (see the card at Luke 2).
